power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) quantify the reliability of measurements made on the same persons by different raters.

In interrater reliability studies, consistency ICCs assess whether scores preserve the relative rankings of persons, while agreement ICCs evaluate the closeness of absolute scores across raters, thereby penalising systematic rater differences.

In two-way mixed-effects designs, where raters are treated as fixed, conventional agreement ICCs raise a conceptual paradox: fixed-rater dispersion contributes to a source of disagreement despite the rater effects being constants, and it remains in the coefficient for all-rater averages even though those effects cancel in the average.
In this paper, we resolve this paradox by introducing a finite-population sampling framework grounded in the correlation approach with hypothetical replications.
Within this framework, we derive correlation-based agreement ICCs for both single ratings and all-rater averages, establishing a coherent probabilistic foundation that resolves the paradox.
By considering various rater-sampling schemes, a family of agreement ICCs in mixed-effects designs is presented.
We further show that the conventional agreement formulas can be recovered under independent sampling with replacement both within and between replicates.
Thus, choosing an appropriate agreement ICC requires specifying how raters are sampled within and across replicates, rather than relying on the design alone.

Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) are widely used to assess reliability in psychology, medicine, and the social sciences, with formulations that distinguish consistency from (absolute) agreement.

The concept of the ICC was originally introduced by fisher1925<empty citation> in the context of analysis of variance (ANOVA), and its contemporary formulation was established through three seminal papers (bartko1966; shrout1979; mcgraw1996) with a very large impact on the scientific literature.

text.text: Despite the ubiquity of these guidelines, the theoretical formulation of agreement under the two-way mixed-effects design remains conceptually contentious.

In two-way mixed-effects designs, where persons are random but raters are treated as fixed, researchers are typically concerned with reliability restricted to a specific, predetermined set of raters, rather than generalising to a broader rater population.
Raters serve as the running example here, but the fixed factor may also represent a specified set of measurement instruments or assessment conditions.
In these settings, an agreement ICC, unlike a consistency ICC, is specifically designed to account for systematic differences

Conceptually and historically, an ICC represents the correlation between scores obtained across two hypothetical replicates for the same target under a specified measurement procedure (shrout1979; bartko1966; vangeneugden2005; barnhart2007; lin2026b).
While this interpretation arises naturally in random-effects designs, it is less straightforward when raters are fixed.

Under the model assumption that rater identities are fixed and known, their effects are unknown constants rather than random variables; consequently, they do not contribute to the probabilistic variation across hypothetical repetitions of the rating procedure.

Consistent with the correlation-based definition, shrout1979<empty citation> presented only consistency coefficients (i.e., ICC(3, 1) and ICC(3, k)), omitting any formulation for agreement (see Table 1).

text.text: In contrast, mcgraw1996<empty citation>, adopting a variance-partitioning rationale, defined agreement coefficients (i.e., ICC(A, 1) and ICC(A, k)) by including the dispersion of fixed rater effects, denoted by θ 2 R , in their denominators as a source of disagreement.

text.text: We refer to this apparent conflict as the fixed-rater agreement paradox, which manifests in two distinct theoretical contradictions: First, for single scores, fixed constants do not vary across replications of an experiment; treating fixed dispersion as a variance component lacks a coherent probabilistic foundation.
Second, and more critically, averaging scores across all K fixed raters yields a rater contribution of 0 (because of the sum-to-zero constraint).
Therefore, no rater-induced variance should remain in the average score.
However, the classical ICC(A, K) formula retains the term θ 2 R /K in the denominator (mcgraw1996).
These contradictions raise fundamental questions regarding the conceptual consistency and theoretical justification of how the ICC is defined.
This conceptual inconsistency extends beyond classical ANOVA frameworks into modern linear mixed-effects models (LMMs).
For instance, vangeneugden2005<empty citation> defined both relative (consistency) and absolute (agreement) reliabilities in LMMs by completely excluding rater variance for fixed effects.
text.formatted: For instance, vangeneugden2005<empty citation> defined both relative (consistency) and absolute (agreement) reliabilities in LMMs by completely excluding rater variance for fixed effects.

text.text: Conversely, nakagawa2017<empty citation> differentiated between an adjusted ICC (excluding fixed-effect variance) and an unadjusted ICC (including it).
text.formatted: Conversely, nakagawa2017<empty citation> differentiated between an adjusted ICC (excluding fixed-effect variance) and an unadjusted ICC (including it).

text.text: The approaches from default in widely used R packages such as irr::icc() (gamer2019) and performance::icc() (luedecke2021), respectively.

These contrasting conventions in ANOVA and LMM frameworks show the lack of theoretical consensus regarding how the dispersion of fixed effects should be conceptualised and quantified in reliability estimation.

These contradictions arise because the two-way mixed-effects model specifies how scores are generated from a given set of raters, whereas a correlation-based definition of the ICC additionally requires a specification of which raters produce the scores in each hypothetical replicate.
The model itself does not determine whether fixed-rater dispersion enters the coefficient.

Accordingly, the central question of this study is: Under what explicitly specified rater-selection and replication mechanisms does fixed-rater dispersion contribute to the variance or covariance of replicate scores?

To resolve this fixed-rater agreement paradox, the present study proposes to use a finite-population sampling framework to clarify the role of fixed-rater dispersion in agreement ICCs for two-way mixed-effects designs.
We treat the K fixed raters of interest as a finite population (rousson2011) and explicitly specify how raters are selected within and between hypothetical replicates.
Using a correlation approach (lin2026b; vangeneugden2005), we then define and derive agreement ICCs under these selection mechanisms.

First, we resolve the fixed-rater agreement paradox by establishing a formal probabilistic foundation for fixed-rater agreement, clarifying how rater dispersion legitimately enters single-score coefficients and why it completely vanishes from all-rater averages.
Second, we generalise the framework to derive a family of agreement ICCs for single and average scores, allowing different numbers of raters and different degrees of rater overlap between replicates.
By linking these coefficients to their underlying selection mechanisms, we provide a basis for choosing a coefficient that matches the intended replication procedure.

Third, we demonstrate that McGraw and Wong's (mcgraw1996) conventional agreement ICC arises when raters are sampled independently with replacement, after accounting for the distinction between the ANOVA-scaled dispersion θ 2 R and the finite-population variance.
This result provides a replication-based interpretation of the conventional formula.
The remainder of the paper is organised as follows.
Section 2 formalises the two-way mixed-effects model and details the algebraic origins of conventional formulas.
Section 3 develops the finite-population resolution for single scores and all-rater averages.

Section 4 generalises this framework to derive a family of agreement ICCs for single scores and averages, allowing different numbers of raters and different degrees of rater overlap between hypothetical replicates.
Finally, Section 5 discusses theoretical and practical implications, offers guidance for applied researchers, and outlines future directions.
2 The fixed-rater agreement paradox in two-way mixed-effects designs
Consider a balanced, fully crossed rating design, where each person is scored by the same set of K raters.
We use an additive two-way mixed-effects model, treating persons as random and raters as fixed.
Inference concerning raters is restricted to these K raters, without assuming that they are sampled from a larger rater population.
In other words, these raters constitute the specific panel of interest, and findings are restricted to this set without generalising to an unobserved rater population.

The model for this design is expressed as: where Y ij is the score assigned to person i by rater j, µ is the grand mean, S i is the random effect for person i, R j is the fixed effect for rater j, and ε ij is the residual error.
S i and ε ij are assumed to be mutually independent with means of zero and finite variances of σ 2 S and σ 2 ε , respectively.
To ensure model identifiability, the rater fixed effects are subject to the sum-to-zero constraint: K j=1 R j = 0.
The rater effects R 1 , . . . , R K are fixed, unknown constants.
In traditional settings, they are not drawn from any probability distribution and therefore do not contribute a random variance component in the model.
Furthermore, because a rater rarely evaluates the same person multiple times in a single setting, a person-by-rater interaction effect cannot be estimated separately from residual error ε ij .

In this paper, we use the term operational score to refer to the score whose reliability is being evaluated and intended for subsequent analysis or decision-making.
Depending on its unit of measurement, an operational score may consist of a single rating or an average of multiple ratings.

Substitution of the expected mean squares under the additive mixed-effects model places θ 2 R in the same algebraic position than the random-rater variance component σ 2 R under the random-effects model.
This correspondence explains how fixed-rater dispersion enters the conventional formula.
This algebraic explanation should be distinguished from a probabilistic interpretation.
In the mixed-effects model, θ 2 R is an ANOVA-scaled measure of dispersion among the K fixed rater effects; it is not the variance component of a random rater effect.

Consequently, the computational equivalence of the estimators does not imply that the random-effects and mixed-effects models define the same population quantity, nor does it specify how fixed-rater dispersion could contribute to the variance or covariance of hypothetical replicate scores.
While mcgraw1996<empty citation> acknowledged that some of their proposed ICCs do not satisfy the strict correlation definition, they emphasised their practical value.

text.text: Under a variance-partitioning interpretation, the dispersion θ 2 R is included in the denominator as a source of disagreement, thereby accounting for systematic differences in rater's severity.
The remaining question is how these differences can contribute to a correlation between replicate scores.
The correlations derived above treat the rater identities as known.
If the rater identity is instead selected at random, the effect entering a score can vary even though each individual rater effect remains a fixed constant.
The following section develops this distinction by introducing an explicit randomisation mechanism over the finite population of K fixed raters.
Before formalising the rater-selection mechanism, it is necessary to distinguish the observed data-collection design from the hypothetical replication protocol defining the ICC.

The observed data matrix (e.g., the fully crossed panel of K raters evaluating n persons in two-way mixed-effects designs) provides the empirical basis for estimating the underlying model parameters (σ 2 S , δ 2 R , and σ 2 ε ).
By contrast, the ICC reflects the hypothetical replication of an operational measurement procedure, specifying how raters from a finite population are assigned to replicates.
Consequently, the observed data structure alone cannot determine a unique agreement ICC.

This insight directly challenges conventional ICC selection flowcharts (shrout1979; mcgraw1996; koo2016), which typically suggest that once the experimental design and model type are identified, the appropriate ICC formula is pinned down.
In reality, the observed design only governs parameter estimation, not the operational replication policy of interest.

In other words, the same fully crossed dataset can legitimately support multiple reliability evaluations across alternative operational protocols, provided the required model parameters are estimable.
Formulating these replication mechanisms and their corresponding agreement ICCs is the focus of this section.

To give fixed-rater dispersion a probability-based interpretation within the correlation approach, we shift the source of randomness from the rater effects themselves to the selection of rater identities.
In a random-effects formulation, each rater effect is a random variable drawn from a specified distribution.

Here, by contrast, each rater effect remains a fixed, unknown constant, and the randomness arises only from the sampling or random assignment of raters from the finite population of K raters of interest.
Consequently, the effect entering a replicate score depends on which rater is selected (rousson2011).

This distinction between fixed effects and random assignment has parallels with randomisation-based inference in experimental design (splawaneyman1990) and finite universes of admissible observations in Generalisability Theory (brennan2001).

Each rater is drawn from R with equal probability and is independent of other random variables, such as person effects and residual errors.
Let J be a random index uniformly selected from {1, . . . , K}.
The selected effect R J is then a random variable, although each R j remains fixed.

When assessing reliability, the dependence between two replicate scores depends critically on how raters are selected.
More generally, let R J h be the random variable representing the rater effect drawn from R in step h (with h = 1, . . . , K).
When considering two distinct replicates h and h ′ (h ̸ = h ′ ), two sampling mechanisms are possible.
If we consider sampling without replacement between replicates, the two replicates are strictly required to use two different raters (i.e., J h ̸ = J h ′ ).
Because the raters are distinct and their total sum is constrained to zero, successive draws are inherently dependent, inducing a negative covariance between any two rater effects R J h and R J h ′ .

This negative covariance can be quantified by expanding the variance of the sum of a complete sequence of K draws without replacement: with the last step being possible because the covariance does not depend on the particular pair that is considered (assuming the raters are different).

Equation 5 demonstrates that sampling fixed effects without replacement inherently induces a negative covariance.
Furthermore, if δ 2 R remains bounded, the covariance approaches zero as K → ∞.
This limiting result indicates that the dependence induced by sampling without replacement becomes negligible for a sufficiently large finite rater population.

Alternatively, if we consider sampling with replacement between replicates, the raters are sampled independently from the finite population R. In this case, the two replicates may happen to select the same rater with probability 1/K. Therefore, the marginal covariance can be decomposed by conditioning on whether the same rater is selected:
The positive covariance resulting from drawing identical raters is precisely offset by the negative covariance induced when drawing distinct raters.

The ICCs for single-scores and all-rater average-scores derived in Section 3 are actually special cases of a broader family of agreement ICCs for two-way mixed-effects designs.
This family is characterised by the number of ratings averaged to form the operational score and the rater-selection mechanisms both within and between (hypothetical) replicates.
We now derive and examine how these features jointly determine the variance and covariance of replicate scores and, consequently, their agreement ICC.
In some empirical research, such as planned-missing and incomplete block designs
The number of raters shared between the two replicates is represented by the overlap variable M = |J 1 ∩ J 2 |, with realised integer values m bounded by max{0, 2k -K} ≤ m ≤ k.

To systematically evaluate reliability for panel-average scores, two distinct sampling dimensions of the hypothetical replication protocol must be distinguished: (1) within-replicate sampling, which specifies how the k raters are drawn from the finite pool R to form a single operational score, and (2) between-replicate rater replacement, which governs how the rater panels assigned across the two hypothetical replicates relate to each other.
In practical rating protocols, under two-way designs, an individual is rarely evaluated multiple times by the exact same rater on a single measurement occasion.
Thus, within-replicate sampling is normally conducted without replacement, ensuring that each operational score is formed by k distinct raters.
Under this protocol, the agreement between replicate scores is governed by the rater replacement mechanism adopted between replicates: 1.
Sampling without replacement (no overlap, m = 0): The two replicates are assigned strictly disjoint rater panels.

In empirical research, this mechanism evaluates cross-panel reproducibility, such as whether an entirely independent team of k clinicians or graders agrees with the initial panel (feasible when k ≤ K/2).
Sampling with partial replacement (partial overlap,1 ≤ m ≤ k): The two replicates are constrained to share exactly m raters.
This protocol models rotating panel designs, such as review committees composed of m permanent chairs and km rotating members.

Sampling with replacement (random overlap, M is random): Rater panels J 1 and J 2 are sampled independently from the finite pool R. This mechanism represents the most general, unconstrained replication policy in practice: when an assessment routinely assigns a random subset of k raters to evaluate each person, a natural replication simply re-runs this random assignment independently, without imposing any constraints on who may be selected again.
Under this policy, the number of shared raters M is random.
To reconcile the conventional agreement ICC definition with the correlation approach, we also consider the theoretical possibility of sampling raters with replacement within each replicate.
Because raters are drawn with replacement within each replicate, replicating the protocol across occasions naturally implies sampling with replacement between replicates as well: 4.

Independent and identically distributed (IID) rater draws: raters contributing to the two replicates are sampled independently and uniformly from {1, . . . , K}, with replacement both within and between replicates (yielding 2k mutually independent draws).

Although rarely implemented in applied rating protocols, under these assumptions, the resulting coefficient has the same algebraic form as the conventional ANOVA-based agreement ICC of mcgraw1996<empty citation>.

The no-overlap mechanism evaluates the agreement between scores obtained from entirely different raters within the same finite pool.
The single-score case (k = 1) is particularly relevant when the comparison specifically targets agreement across distinct raters or measurement methods.

This requirement distinguishes agreement between different methods from agreement under independent method selection, which permits the same method to be selected for both replicates.

text.text: In practice, researchers assign a random subset of k raters to evaluate each target under a standardised operational procedure.

Equation 17 is structurally identical to McGraw and Wong's (mcgraw1996) conventional agreement ICC for two-way mixed-effects models, after replacing their ANOVA-scaled rater dispersion θ 2 R with the finite-population variance δ 2 R .
This result reveals that the conventional formula can be recovered from the correlation approach as if raters are drawn with replacement from the finite pool.
Despite this structural equivalence, the sampling protocol is substantively implausible.
Sampling raters with replacement within a replicate allows the same rater to be selected repeatedly while others in the finite pool are omitted.

For example, an all-rater average from a committee of K = 3 raters (k = K = 3) could consist of one rater scoring the same person two or three times at the same occasion while the other raters are excluded entirely.
No practitioner would construct an "all-rater average" this way; operational panels of size k are always formed by sampling distinct raters without replacement.
Crucially, when all K raters are deployed in practice (k = K), the operational protocol constitutes a panel census rather than an IID sample: every rater evaluates the target exactly once.
Under the sum-to-zero constraint, the fixed rater effects cancel out identically across persons, leaving zero rater variance in the operational average score.

Thus, the persistence of the rater dispersion term θ 2 R /K in McGraw and Wong's conventional formula (or the rater variance term δ 2 R /K in Equation 17) is not the reflection of a realistic replication policy.

text.text: The present paper provides an explicit probabilistic account of how fixed-rater dispersion contributes to agreement ICCs in two-way mixed-effects designs.
In conventional formulations (mcgraw1996), the absolute agreement ICC under a two-way mixed-effects model incorporates the fixed-rater dispersion into the denominator as a source of disagreement.
However, this specification is at odds with the idea that an ICC is a correlation.
Specifically, the rater effect is constant across persons and replicates, contributing neither variance nor covariance regardless of parameterisation.
In addition, the fixed-rater dispersion shows up even in all-rater average scores, which is problematic because the fixed effects parameters sum to zero.

The conventional framework leaves two fundamental issues unresolved: (1) the rationale for defining fixed-rater dispersion using an ANOVA-scaled mean square rather than a proper population variance, and (2) the absence of a direct derivation grounding these coefficients in the classical definition of the ICC as a correlation between hypothetical replicates.
To resolve these issues, we propose a finite-population framework that clarifies the random mechanism through which fixed-rater effects may or may not enter replicates.
Randomness arises from the assignment mechanism that pairs specific raters with persons.

Under this setting, we formally define the finite population variance of the fixed rater effects , allowing agreement ICCs to be derived directly as correlations between two replicates for the same target person.
When replicates are formed by averaging ratings from k raters sampled without replacement from a finite panel of K raters, the variance of the observed average score is: (FPC) factor.

The incorporation of the FPC provides a natural and mathematically coherent transition: for single-rater scores (k = 1), the full rater dispersion enters the error term; as the operational score expands to the entire panel (k = K), the FPC reduces to zero, and rater dispersion naturally vanishes.
By articulating the joint selection mechanisms both within and between replicates, we establish a comprehensive family of agreement ICCs for two-way mixed-effects designs.
A central implication of our framework is that the observational rating design alone does not determine a unique correlation-based agreement ICC.

Standard statistical software often creates the impression that in case of a two-way mixed design and the aim of assessing absolute agreement uniquely specifies the formula to be used, such as in mcgraw1996<empty citation>.

text.text: In reality, a fully crossed observational dataset merely supplies the empirical quantities necessary to estimate person, rater, and residual variance components.

The actual target coefficient depends fundamentally on how the operational score (e.g., a single rating, the average rating of all raters, or the average rating of some subset of raters) is constructed and how its hypothetical replication is conceived (e.g., can the same rater be sampled again in the hypothetical replication or not?).
Consequently, the same empirical dataset can generate distinct agreement coefficients depending on the research question.
To ensure valid interpretation and reproducibility, researchers adopting a mixed-effects agreement ICC must explicitly specify their operational protocol.

Specifically, reporting should detail: (1) the finite rater population of interest K, (2) the number of ratings averaged to form the operational score k, (3) the within-replicate rater-selection mechanism, and (4) the between-replicate assignment rule, including the extent of rater overlap across replicates (e.g., whether replicates draw identical, partially shared, or strictly distinct raters).
Explicitly documenting these choices aligns the statistical coefficient with its intended measurement context while keeping population inferences properly grounded within the defined fixed panel.
The extent of rater overlap between replicates M critically shapes how agreement is interpreted within our proposed family.

When the finite rater size K and the number of raters per score k are held constant, reducing the overlap systematically decreases the covariance between replicate scores whenever fixed-rater differences are present, while the marginal variance of each replicate remains unchanged.
This decrease in covariance arises because drawing distinct raters from a zero-sum fixed panel inherently induces a negative covariance between their effects.
In the extreme case of requiring strictly distinct raters (M = 0), when feasible, this negative dependence is maximised.
When fixed-rater dispersion is substantial relative to target (i.e., person) variation, this negative covariance can produce a negative population ICC.
Crucially, such negative values are an intrinsic consequence of the finite-sampling assignment mechanism, rather than artifactual sample noise or negative variance estimates.
Conversely, increasing the overlap raises the covariance because shared rater effects contribute positively to the covariance between replicates.
Consequently, an elevated coefficient under higher overlap indicates greater stability when raters are retained, rather than greater agreement among distinct raters.
Finally, our derivations provide a correlation-based interpretation of the agreement ICCs in mixed-effects designs.
Such a correlation-based interpretation lies at the origin of the ICC (bartko1966; shrout1979) and can be easily found in random-effect designs.
Recently, Lin et al. (lin2025; lin2026) have generalised it to more complex designs with random effects.
Unfortunately, mixed-effect designs have long remained a blind spot.
Though the conventional mixed-effects agreement coefficients do not satisfy the strict correlation definition, the results in this paper now fill this gap.

The conventional formula can be recovered only under independent sampling with replacement both within and between replicates (Section 4.3), a protocol that is difficult to justify for panel averages because it permits the same rater to be selected repeatedly.

This study develops a correlation-based framework for agreement ICCs in two-way mixed-effects designs by explicitly specifying rater assignment from a finite fixed panel.
Although individual rater effects remain fixed, random assignment allows their dispersion to contribute to replicate-score variance and covariance.
The framework clarifies the fixed-rater agreement paradox and yields a family of agreement ICCs indexed by the scoring unit and replication mechanism.
Selecting and interpreting an agreement ICC therefore requires specifying how raters are sampled within and assigned between hypothetical replicates.

It will become evident in the context of all-rater average scores, McGraw and Wong's formulation relies heavily on an ANOVA-based variance partitioning philosophy, rather than an explicit conceptualisation of independent rater reassignment.3.3 Agreement ICC for all-rater average scoresNext, we consider the all-rater (full-panel) average score, defined as the mean of the ratings provided by all K fixed raters.
The key distinction from the single-score case is not averaging itself, but that the all-rater average score exhausts the finite rater population.
For single scores, the researcher has the freedom to specify whether the rater is assigned either with or without replacement between replicates.
By contrast, when the operational score is the average of the entire finite set of K raters, this freedom vanishes.

The replicate average scores for person i are then Ȳi• = µ + S i + RJ 1 + εi• and this study provides a new perspective on agreement ICCs, several limitations and avenues for future work remain.
First, the proposed agreement ICCs assume an additive linear model, homogeneous residual variances, and independent residual errors across hypothetical replicates.
With one observation per person-rater cell, person-by-rater interactions cannot be separated from residual error.
However, it does not mean the interactions are absent or independent across replicates.

Under the model specification, person-by-rater interactions must sum to zero across the fixed panel for each person K j=1 (SR) ij = 0, which inherently forces a negative covariance between distinct raters evaluating the same target (bartko1974; shrout1979).

If these interaction effects persist systematically across replicates, assigning non-overlapping raters will inject additional negative covariance into replicate scores, whereas forming an all-rater average (k = K) causes the interaction to cancel out entirely.

Future work should model these interactions explicitly and examine their implications under different rater-replacement policies.Second, this study establishes theoretical population ICCs rather than evaluating the finite-sample performance of their estimators.

Although the required variance components can be estimated via ANOVA moments, restricted maximum likelihood, or Bayesian techniques (hove2024; hove2025), comprehensive evaluation of these estimators remains an essential next step.
Future research should examine their finite-sample sampling distributions, bias, and efficiency, while developing robust interval estimation via delta-method or bootstrap procedures.
In parallel, Bayesian implementations must incorporate the sum-to-zero identifiability constraint through appropriate prior specifications and evaluate posterior sensitivity (rouder2012; hove2020).

Finally, extending existing precision-and power-based sample-size planning frameworks (mondal2025; mondal2025b) to the proposed fixed-panel coefficients will provide crucial practical guidance for empirical design.
Third, translating the proposed agreement ICC family into research practice introduces unique challenges.
Several coefficients, such as those conditioning on a fixed rater overlap (M = m), are relatively new in the reliability literature.

Because empirical studies have rarely documented hypothetical replication mechanisms, future research should establish a comprehensive selection guideline and decision workflow, accompanied by concrete worked examples.
